## Abstract

The electronic structure of the carbon-based nanomaterials can be modulated by doping

heteroatoms into them. When nitrogen is doped into the graphene structure with different

bonding configurations, it changes the material's electronic properties in a variety of ways.

Because of the tuned electronic properties, nitrogen-doped graphene (N-G) is applicable in

electrochemical systems as catalyst. Despite having tremendous prospects, a holistic view of

the structural and functional properties of N-G is still unclear. Moreover, to our knowledge,

significant findings on the properties of N-G are not well documented yet, which creates an

obstacle to the further improvement of this nanomaterial. Keeping our focus on the catalytic

activities, in this paper, we presented an in-detailed review of the overall chemical structure

and functional properties of N-G nanomaterials. Starting from the structural properties of

major precursor materials for N-G synthesis, we reviewed the physical features and its

dependence on the synthesis parameters. Also, a detailed study has been conducted on the

key nitrogen functional groups’ structural properties, favorable formation environment,

influence on the electronic structure of N-G, and role in the catalytic activity. Current

progress on the stability of N-G nanocatalysts is reported with an insight into the degradation

mechanism.

Keywords: Nitrogen-doped graphene, Catalyst, Structural property, Electronic property,

Stability, Degradation mechanism.

## 1. Introduction:

Among the naturally occurring allotropes of carbon, graphite is the most common and stable

one under standard conditions. Graphite forms as stacked-up layers of carbon and the

individual layers are known as graphene. Ideally, graphene is a one-atom-thick true two-

dimensional material with hexagonal honeycomb-shaped lattices of sp2 hybridized carbon

atoms.  Thanks to graphene’s unique chemical, mechanical, and electrical properties, it has

drawn the attention of a good many disciplines of technology although the synthesis of

graphene is a comparatively new development [1]. High mechanical strength and corrosion

resistance emerge from the strong σ bonds between the sp2 hybridized orbitals of the carbon

atoms in the graphene network. As documented, graphene has Young’s modulus of ∼1 TPa, a

surface area of 2630 m2/g, and around 5000 W/mK of thermal conductivity [2–4]. Also, the

long-range π-bond system of graphene provides the potential for various electrochemical

applications with a charged carrier mobility of about 200000 cm2V−1s−1 [4]. Despite

possessing all these appealing properties graphene in its pristine form exhibits an inert

characteristic with a zero energy band gap between its conduction and valance bands [5]. It is

desirable to modulate its properties by introducing impurities of any kind; either by creating

structural defects or doping foreign atoms/functional groups. these defects disrupt the

graphene’s pristine structure and hence an overlapping between the energy bands is

generated, which in turn activates the graphene for different applications. Similar to

semiconductor doping, heteroatoms like nitrogen (N), boron (B), and sulfur (S) doping into

the graphene lattice is a popular practice to tune its electronic properties [6,7]. While B

doping generates a p-type effect in the material, N-doped graphene can achieve both p-type

and n-type properties depending on the dominant type of nitrogen functional group present in

the structure [5,8]. For such excellent prospect of tunability nitrogen-doped graphene (N-G)

is extensively studied by numerous research groups given the focus on its morphology,

chemical compositions, electronic properties, etc. aiming toward various applications. Before

designing any specific target-oriented N-G nanomaterials, it is imperative to fully understand

their morphology, structural and electronic properties in different environments.

One of the most notable applications of N-G nanomaterials is their usability as a catalyst in

electrochemical systems. Many research groups, focused on fuel cell materials, trying to

replace the commonly used Platinum (Pt)-based catalysts because of their high cost and CO

poisoning issues. N-G has emerged as a highly potential candidate to replace Pt from the

electrochemical systems due to their enhanced catalytic activity for oxygen reduction reaction

(ORR) [9–18]. It is to be noted that Platinum was found to be the most effective catalyst

for electrochemical systems due to its unique electronic configuration. With similar

electronic configurations, Platinum group metals (Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir) show noticeable

catalytic activity. A key step for the ORR mechanism is the adsorption of O2 on the

metal site and subsequence breaking of the O=O bond. For Pt or Pt group metal

catalysts, excess electrons in their d orbital are back donated to the antibonding π

orbitals of adjacent adsorbed oxygen molecules (pi back donation/ pi back bonding)

which weakens the O=O bond and eventually breaks the bond [19–22]. Such a catalytic

mechanism can be contrasted with the electronic activities in N-G nanomaterials.

Although such mechanisms for N-G catalysts are not extensively studied yet,

modification of graphene’s electronic structure (described in later sections) due to

nitrogen doping enables the materials to act as electrochemical catalysts. Numerous

experimental, theoretical, and numerical investigations already established the role of

N-G materials as electrochemical catalysts. Therefore, it is more appropriate to mention

that N-G materials can play the role of electrochemical catalysts although they may not

follow the exact electronic activities as Pt or Pt-based or Pt group metal catalysts do. For

such property, N-G nanomaterials are also being studied as catalysts as well as electrode

materials for Metal-air batteries [23–26]. N-G can act as excellent anode materials for

Lithium-ion batteries. The pyridinic-N functional groups in N-G lower the energy barrier for

Li diffusion which results in an increased performance of the Lithium-ion batteries [27–30].

Also, this new nanomaterial open new possibility for light emitting diodes [31,32], field-

effect transistors [33,34], medical devices [35–42], supercapacitors [43–45], magnetic

memory [46], photonics [28], photocatalyst [8]. All the application-oriented studies on N-G

nanomaterials included the investigation of the structural and electrochemical properties as

they are the key to decode the full potential of this propitious material.

Through numerous investigations on different aspects of the N-G nanomaterials for different

applications, some consensuses were reached over the chemical structure, morphology,

electronic structure, identification of catalytically active sites, and functionalities.

Nonetheless, many fundamental debates over its structural properties and functionalities are

still on the table. An up-to-date and detailed review of the overall chemical and physical

structure, properties, and catalytic activities of the N-G nanomaterials is unavailable, which

simultaneously discusses both agreements and disagreements over different properties to

6

show the current state of development. Such a review could shed light on the overall picture

of N-G nanomaterials research. In this review, we have presented a clear overview of the

chemical structure to the molecular scale, morphology, electronic properties, catalytic

functionality, as well as catalytic stability and degradation-related issues of the N-G

nanocatalyst. First, we elucidate the structural properties of the major precursors for N-G

synthesis as N-G nanomaterials inherit the basic structural features from them. Precursors are

often used as a tool to modulate the properties of N-G products. Then we presented a brief

review on the physical properties of N-Gs, their dependence on synthesis parameters and

derived an overall structural view of N-G. It is well established that different nitrogen

functional groups generate unique catalytic activity and play distinct roles in the performance

and stability of the catalyst. Hence, we conducted an in-detailed review on major nitrogen

functional groups in N-G nanomaterials: pyrrolic-N, pyridinic-N, graphitic-N, and often

found pyridinic-N oxide. We have also reported the developments on the stability issues of

N-G nanocatalysts and their degradation mechanism.

## 2. Review on Precursor Materials for N-G nanomaterial Synthesis:

### 2.1 Major Carbon Precursors:

To acquire a decent understanding of how the N-G nanomaterials take their unique structural

orientations and exhibit electrochemical catalytic activity, it is essential to review the

structural features and properties of the commonly used precursor materials for N-G

synthesis. N-G nanomaterials inherit the structural base from the graphene-derived carbon

precursors. Graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), being the only

derivatives of graphene that can be synthesized in kilogram scales, are commonly used as the

carbon precursor in different N-G synthesis methods [47]. In this subsection, we will mainly

focus on the structural features and notable properties of GO and rGO.

Graphene oxide (GO):

Although dated back in the 1850’s Brodie first prepared and described GO, its potential of

providing an alternative path to produce graphene was recognized after the first synthesis and

graphene’s tremendous prospects were unveiled [1,47–55]. From a basic perspective GO

structure is regarded as a graphene sheet with different oxygen-containing groups bonded on


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

the surface. However, the most accepted Lerf−Klinowski model described the GO basal plane

decorated with adsorbed hydroxy and epoxy groups while the plane edges are ended by

carboxy functional groups. These oxygen functional groups alter the sp2 hybridized carbon

atoms of the graphene into sp3 hybridized ones. Such sp2 to sp3 conversion of the carbon

atoms distorts the graphene basal plane [56–58]. Later Gao et al. modified the model by

confirming the presence of five- and six-membered lactol (O-C-O) rings, ester of tertiary

alcohol, hydroxyl, epoxy, and ketone functionalities on the GO plane [59]. Fig.1 shows a

structural model derived from the proposal of Gao et al. Concomitantly, through direct

observation of the GO surface, alongside distorted sp3 regions with adsorbed oxygen groups,

defect-free sp2 graphene regions, also other structural defects (holes, pentagonal-heptagonal-

inversed hexagonal ring regions) were located [48,49,51]. Meanwhile, Dimiev et al. proposed

the dynamic structural model (DSM) of GO where they demonstrated that the structure

undergoes gradual changes in the aqueous solution by interacting with water and generates

the acidic nature which was observed previously [60].

In an investigation on the local chemical structure of GO and rGO Erickson et al. presented

transmission electron microscope (TEM) images of monolayer GO sheet and they

distinguished three major features on the GO surface: highly oxidized distorted region,

unoxidized graphitic region, and holes. These three regions occupied 82%, 16%, and 2% of

the surface area of the GO sample respectively [51]. Similar surface features were observed

in the studies of Dave et al. and Pacilé et al., however, the size of these contrasted regions

depends on the oxidation processes and exfoliation conditions [47,52,55]. In the distorted

region, adsorbates are weakly bonded and get desorbed if heated over 500⁰C. Also, the

incident electron beam from TEM can remove the adsorbates from the GO surface [47,51].

Marsden et al. suggested that while the oxygen functionalities are desorbed from the

graphene plane at high temperature, the opposite happens for the nitrogen functional groups;

substitutional nitrogen groups in the graphene lattice increase significantly with annealing

temperature. They also found that the physisorbed molecular oxygens do not bring any

significant change to the electronic structure of graphene [53].

Mkhoyan et al. measured the thicknesses of GO single layer and multilayers employing

atomic force microscopy (AFM) and composition sensitive annular dark field (ADF)

imaging. The thickness ratio of mono-, bi-, and trylayers of GO were found 1: 1.5: 2 instead

of 1: 2: 3, which indicates an ununiform surface roughness that emerged from the C-O bonds

on both sides of the surface. The surface roughness is at least 6 nm. This roughness accounted

for both C-O bond length (maximum 3 nm) and distortion-produced undulations of the basal

plane [48]. The density functional theory (DFT) calculations also support the above-described

surface structure and GO layers’ morphology [50].

The above-discussed structural and morphological features generate various unique

properties in GO. The electric conductivity of GO is lower than the pristine graphene by a

factor of 10-100 (quantified less than 10-10 Scm-1). This near insulating characteristic is

governed by the portion of the distorted region with oxygen groups. The sp3 hybridized

carbon atoms in that region act as insulators with a wide band gap [55,59]. The unoxidized

graphitic regions on the GO plane cause notable broadband fluorescence. The presence of

carboxyl groups at the edges and hydroxyl and epoxy groups on the basal plane of GO makes

room for the chemical modifications through different targeted reactions. In this way,

application-specified (drug delivery, biodevices, polymer composite) functional groups can

be conjugated with the GO [55,61].

Reduced graphene oxide (rGO):

Reduction of GO was attempted by thermal, chemical, and hybrid methods. These attempts

were successful in increasing the sp2 regions of GO hence the electrical conductance and

electron mobility of the substance increased. However, complete restoration of the graphene

structure from GO could not be attained as substantial inhomogeneous structures of the basal

plane were retained. Also, the formation of stable groups as carbonyl on GO blocked the path

of graphene’s full restoration [55]. For such reasons these substances cannot take the place of

epitaxial chemical vapor deposition (CVD) graphene, hence, they are commonly referred to

as reduced graphene oxide (rGO). Nonetheless, rGO was found to process higher electrical

conductivity up to 4 order than GO, also the aspect of controllable functionality, economic

Other commonly used carbon precursors for N-G synthesis:

Literature shows many other carbon precursor materials are utilized for N-G synthesis.

Synthesis method like CVD generally requires the use of gaseous precursors with a

controllable flow rate. Methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2), etc. gases are

commonly used in this method. Variation in the flow rate of carbon precursors can

manipulate the content of nitrogen functional groups present on the N-G materials. In some

cases of CVD, gaseous 1,3,5-triazine [62], pyridine (C5H5N) [63,64], acetonitrile (CH3CN)

[5], etc. are used as both carbon and nitrogen sources.

### 2.2 Major Nitrogen Precursors:

Choice of nitrogen precursors is one of the factors that largely influences the synthesis as

well as functional properties of N-G nanomaterials [6,65]. Depending on the synthesis

methods different nitrogen sources are utilized. In the CVD method, as gaseous precursors

are generally used, ammonia (NH3), nitrogen gas (N2) gases [66] are used commonly. While

N2 readily available and comparatively easy to supply to the CVD chamber, the use of NH3

requires taking additional measures for handling the substance because of its toxic nature. In

general, with these nitrogen sources, 4–16 at% nitrogen doping can be achieved in N-G

nanomaterials by CVD methods [67].

In thermal annealing and heat treatment methods, solid nitrogen precursors are often used.

Solid nitrogen precursors are advantageous in terms of their capability to supply high

nitrogen content volumetrically. For an instance, melamine (C3H6N6) is a white organic

compound with 67% nitrogen content by mass also it is nontoxic. Common choice for solid

nitrogen precursors in thermal annealing and heat treatment processes are Melamine [68,69],

urea [70,71], cyanamide (CH2N2) [72], aminoterephthalic acid [6], imidazole [69], etc.

Reports showed that heat treatment and thermal annealing produced N-G nanomaterials have

a nitrogen content of 7.1–10.1 at% and 3–5 at% respectively. However, in the simple one-

step method of nanoscale high energy wet (NHEW) ball milling, melamine is used as the

source of nitrogen. Following this synthesis method, Zhuang et al. synthesized N-G

nanocatalyst and the nitrogen doping was found as high as 10.28–32.74 at% [67,73–77].

In the low-temperature synthesis process as plasma treatment, N2 plasma is used for nitrogen

doping on pre-prepared carbon sources as graphene, GO, rGO [78–84]. In such a process

typical nitrogen content is found 3–8.5 at% [67]. The nitrogen doping here largely depends

on the strength of the applied N2 plasma and exposure time.

3. Review on Physical Characteristics, Effects of Synthesis Parameters, and Structural Properties of N-G nanomaterials:

### 3.1 Physical Characteristics:

In literature similarities and some differences in the physical forms, morphological and

topological features are reported for the N-G nanomaterials derived through different

synthesis methods and production environments. It is advantageous to be informed of such

physical characteristics of N-Gs produces from the most commonly used approaches:

chemical vapor deposition (CVD), thermal annealing, heat treatment, plasma treatment, ball

milling, etc.

N-G layers are grown on metal substrates (commonly Cu, Ni) inside a reaction chamber/tube

furnace of CVD systems and generally takes the form of thin films, also referred to as N-G

nanosheets. To the bare eyes, N-G nanomaterials are of black or ash color.  As different

groups used a variety of carbon and nitrogen sources, as well as different reaction

temperatures and pressures in their CVD methods, the N-G deposited in layers varies in


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

number. With the current progress of synthesis methods it possible to produce a few layers

(less than 10) to even a single layer of N-G nanomaterial [5,8,62–64,66,85]. Wei et al.

determined the interlayer gap is about 0.34 nm. By analyzing the high resolution transmission

electron microscopy (HRTEM) images they described the N-G layers as crumpled paper with

a variety of defects; such topological features indicate the flexibility of the N-G films [5].

Through the electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) mapping images of CVD produced N-

G, Son et al. confirmed a uniform distribution of the doped nitrogen atoms in graphene [63].

Similar morphological and topological characteristics are found for N-G nanomaterials

synthesized by the thermal annealing and heat treatment methods [6,65,68–72]. The findings

of Li et al. show the change in the surface topology of N-G nanomaterials is directly related

to the applied annealing temperature; the quantitative presence of different nitrogen function

group changes [86]. Physical features were found similar for thermally annealed N-Gs

synthesized by other groups [86–91]. Lu et al. described the morphology of their thermally

annealed nitrogen-doped reduced graphene oxide (N-rGO) as closely associated crumpled

sheets that formed a disordered solid structure. They attributed such features to the

breakdown of graphene lattice during exfoliation and the presence of different nitrogen

functional groups. Interlayer separation for their N-rGO was 0.339 nm [89]. As the heat

treatment method can utilize solid precursors for both carbon and nitrogen, synthesized N-Gs

were reported to have higher nitrogen content on average [65,68–72]. Following the

morphological studies of Haque et al., Ngidi et al., and Sheng et al., it is found that interlayer

spacing between N-G layers can vary depending on the heat treatment temperature; ranges

from 0.34 nm – 0.46 nm for the temperature range of 600⁰C – 1000 ⁰C. However, this

interlayer spacing and heat treatment temperature do not maintain a linear trend [6,65,68]. It

is worth noting that interlayer spacing of commonly used carbon source GO is around 0.47

nm and it is reduced while subjected to heat treatment or annealing for nitrogen doping

[6,68].

N-G nanomaterials synthesized through N2 plasma treatment inherit most of the physical

characteristics from their carbon precursors GO, rGO, or graphene produced by the CVD

method [78–84,92]. Besides, Park et al. noted that the sputtering damage on the N2 plasma-

generated N-G surface is unavoidable [79]. From the topological point of view, overall

nitrogen content and the presence of different nitrogen functional groups critically depend on

the plasma exposure time. Doping nitrogen into graphene can also be achieved by ion

implantation/irradiation. Cress et al., Zhao et al. applied such technique and they

13

observed randomly distributed substitutional nitrogen dopants in their N-G specimens.

It was found that through such energetic ion implementation method, doping of

heteroatoms on graphene layers can be achieved in a more controlled manner so that

the materials can be prepared for a variety of applications. The topological and

morphological features of N-G nanomaterials produced by this method are similar to

the ones synthesized through other methods described earlier [93,94]. Laser-

scribing/engraving of precursor materials is another technique to produce N-G

materials [95–97]. Again, N-G nanomaterials produced through this process show

similar physical forms as previously described. Simultaneous graphene exfoliation and

nitrogen doping is also a common route to produce N-G nanomaterials.

Physical features of N-G nanomaterials synthesized by the high-energy ball milling approach

are somewhat different because the energy required for breaking the strong sp2 C-C bonds in

graphene lattice and nitrogen doping is provided by the kinetic energy of moving solid metal

or ZrO2 balls inside a sealed milling jar [98–105]. Due to the mechanical breakdown of

graphene’s honeycomb carbon structure, plenty of edge defects are formed. As produced

dangling carbon bonds at the edges are highly reactive; the broken zigzag and armchair-

shaped edges can spontaneously facilitate the bonding of the nitrogen atoms to the graphene

structure with the binding energy of -57.65 and -45.20 Kcal/N2 mol respectively [98,99]. The

particle size of the N-G materials can be rendered less than 1μm by the ball milling process

and they exhibit a sponge-like porosity with lower surface area. Similar physical

characteristics are present in the N-G nanomaterials by wet ball milling methods [73,74,106–

108].

For N-G nanomaterials formed by few other direct synthesis methods as the segregation

growth method, arc-discharge method, solvothermal method, structure and morphology are

pretty close to the N-Gs produced by the methods discussed above [109–111]. It was found

that N-G produced by the segregation growth approach exhibits a uniform, largescale,

uniform structure. To note, the scale of N-G materials produced by the arc-discharge

technique is generally below 1μm, and the solvothermal method synthesized N-Gs mainly

consist of 1−6 layers [87].

Often for different applications, it becomes necessary to create vacancy or hole type

defect on graphene-based materials. Irradiation of energetic ion beams is one of the

common ways to do so. Different research groups studied the defect formation


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

mechanisms and revealed that the substrate used to support graphene plays an

important role during the formation of defects especially when the defects are

introduced by the ion irradiation process [112–115]. Li et al. through their experimental

and simulation study reported that substrate materials that have higher thermal

conductance have lower defect yield from ion irradiation on the material. They

experimentally compared the defect yield through irradiation of 6 MeV Si ions (5×105

ions/cm2) on graphene supported on two different substrates: SiO2 and Cu. Defect yield

was much less on graphene supported on Cu than the graphene on SiO2 substrate. Such

difference in defect yield was observed because of the higher thermal conductance of

Copper than SiO2 [113]. This finding provides an idea about the consideration of

substrate material to use as the support for application-specific graphene-based

materials.

To study the defects and their effect on the properties of graphene-based material

including N-G is of interest. Feicht et al. described different defect types that are often

observed in GO. Any deviation from the ideal hexagonal honeycomb lattice they

referred to as in-plane lattice defect [54]. From this perspective, all the functional

groups, structural deformities of any kind present in the N-G structure can be regarded

as defects in general. Defects of any kind change the fundamental electronic structure of

the material and hence changes its properties. Radchenko et al. investigated the

contribution of different nitrogen-doping configurations accompanied by vacancies to

the conductive properties of graphene [116]. Formation, detection, or healing of defects

in N-G materials are the subject of broad research areas of their own accord. From a

general point of view, physical defects like structural deformation, creation of vacancies

produced by mechanical stress, ion bombardment, etc. can lead to the formation of

chemical defects in the form of different fictional groups on the graphene structure.

Different innovative approaches have been developed to controllably produce defects

and thus modulate the properties of graphene-based materials. For instance, Kato et al.

used ultraviolet (UV) range energy of the photon and reactive oxygen species to produce

micropores and reconstruction type (deformed hexagon, pentagon, heptagon produced

in the process of vacancy defect’s healing) defects into a monolayer of graphene [117].

Martín-Recio et al. claimed to achieve control over the doping level and corrugation on

the graphene layer supported on Rh substrate by combining nitrogen doping and

oxygen intercalation [118]. Pan et al. took an interesting approach to heal the defects in


<!-- Page 15 -->


15

graphene by treating with ascorbic acid (vitamin C) followed by thermal annealing of

2950⁰ C. This approach could assist in tuning the properties of N-G materials [119].

Detection and quantification of the defects in graphene-based materials are also

significant. Kim et al. proposed a non-destructive approach (amplitude-modulated

discharge current analysis) to measure the energy levels of defects in graphene [120].

3.2 Doping Effects, Effects of Synthesis Parameters, and Structural Overview of N-G nanomaterials:

As mentioned earlier, the use of graphene in practical applications requires modifications in

its electronic structure. A common approach for such modifications is doping of different

heteroatoms: boron, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, fluorine, bromine, silicon,

germanium, etc. [6,121]. For tuning the properties of graphene, besides the overall

concentration of the dopants, specific bong configurations they form with the graphene

structure are also a significant factor. With distinct atomic structures and chemistry, different

heteroatoms bond with the carbon atoms of graphene lattice uniquely and form specific

bonding configurations and hance modify the doped graphene’s properties in different ways.

Doping of boron atoms into the graphene generates a p-type effect in the material as boron

atoms have one electron less than a carbon atom. When heteroatoms like silicon and

germanium, which are relatively larger in atomic radii than carbon, are doped into graphene,

a single heteroatom can replace two carbon atoms. More electronegative halogen atoms form

bonds with graphene sp3 in nature [121]. Doping nitrogen atoms into graphene is of special

interest as it can form several bonding configurations with graphene: directly substituting a

carbon atom of the lattice (graphitic-N), bonding with two carbon atoms of a six-membered

ring accompanied by vacancies (pyridinic-N), forming a five-membered ring (pyrrolic-N),

creating partially oxidized pyridinic formation (pyridinic-N-O), forming a triple bond with a

carbon atom of the graphene’s zigzag edge (nitrilic-N), etc. Each of these bonding

configurations modulates the electronic structure of graphene lattice uniquely, therefore, their

functionalities are different. Major ones from these configurations will be discussed in detail

in the next section.

Effects of different synthesis parameters: Investigation of the effects of dopants on graphene

is comparatively simple than the doping of silicon-based semiconductors because unlike Si

wafers graphene does not stay in a bulk structure, also dopants are incorporated into graphene

graphene (or GO, rGO) using suitable nitrogen precursors or by post-treatment of with

nitrogen sources after the synthesis of graphene (or GO, rGO). The properties of N-G

nanomaterials critically depend on the synthesis process. Choice of precursors used, applied

temperature and pressure, precursor flow rate, the substrate used, etc. are generally the

controlling parameters for N-Gs synthesis. The underlying growth process largely depends on

the mechanism of decomposition of the precursor molecules and their simultaneous diffusion

to the substrates [121]. By producing N-G materials through CVD from different aromatic

nitrogen-containing precursors Katoh et al. reported that the molecules with the highest

activation barrier for dissociation of aromatic rings produce N-Gs of the highest dopant

concentrations [122]. Aromatic molecules with lower bond energy break easily and form

volatile molecules like HCN and get removed from the system, hence, the overall doped

nitrogen content is reduced. Post doping of nitrogen after graphene synthesis is generally

done by exposing pristine graphene or its derivatives (GO, rGO) to chemically active

nitrogen sources at elevated temperatures, or bombardment by ion gun, or applying nitrogen

plasma. The underlying mechanisms of such post-treatment processes are first creating

defects on graphene lattice by the activity of high-energy nitrogen particles and then

replacing the carbon atoms with nitrogen atoms. In the case of post-treatment synthesis of N-

Gs, the range of elevated temperature, doping/exposure time, the energy of plasma plays a

vital role in determining the dopant concentration and bonding configurations in the produced

materials. Akada et al. and Rybin et al. found that at lower plasma exposure time (about 15s)

graphitic-N group dominates, as exposure time increases pyridinic-N component forms

rapidly, and for longer than 2 min plasma exposure pyrrolic-N group increases [80,92].

However, the majority of studies on post-treatment synthesis of N-G materials reported a

substantial dominance of graphitic-N bonding configuration. High energy ball milling (both

dry and wet) methods for N-G synthesis are also regarded as a post-treatment approach.

Zhuang et al. synthesized different N-G nanocatalysts using nanoscale high energy wet

(NHEW) ball milling method [73,74,123,124]. Pyridinic-N, graphitic-N, pyrrolic-N,

pyridinic-N-oxides nitrogen bonding were detected in their samples. They demonstrated that

grinding time and speed play a key role to control the formation of the detected nitrogen

functional groups. It is generally agreed that through post-synthesis methods more control

over the formation of targeted nitrogen-graphene bonding configurations can be achieved.

Positional presence of functional groups: The studies on N-G nanocatalysts primarily focus

on the major nitrogen functional groups. These groups stay embedded on the basal plane of

the carbon network, however, each of them preferentially gets adsorbed on the energetically

favorable locations of the graphene lattice. Graphitic-N forms by directly replacing a single

carbon atom of the hexagonal honeycomb lattice. They are generally found on positions

surrounded by pure graphene-like structures. From Lin et al.’s inspection of the low

magnification annular dark field (ADF) images of N-G prepared by applying O3 and N2

same hexagonal carbon ring; the distance between two closest graphitic-N configurations was

nitrogen (graphitic-N) configurations can take different positional orientations in the

honeycomb lattice of graphene. Generally, it is expected that the graphitic-N groups are

found randomly distributed over the graphene surface. However, through the STM images’

observation of N-G samples, Zhao et al. found a strong tendency of graphitic-N groups to

form clusters in the same sublattice of graphene [127].

were reported to be accompanied by a single vacancy, double vacancies, triple vacancies, and

even four vacancies. They are also located on the edges of the N-G plane. Pyridinic-N bonds

can be found to exist in side-by-side rings with vacancies. During the synthesis as the

vacancies are generated at random locations, pyridinic-N configurations are expected to be

distributed randomly over the surface. The five-membered ring configured pyrrolic-N groups

are commonly located at the edges of the N-G plane. As the pyridinic-N-oxide configuration

take references from the physical characteristics section where N-G is described as distorted

film-like material with a variety of defects. The planer distortions are most knowingly formed

precursors, some oxygen functional groups as hydroxyl, carboxyl, epoxy, etc. are likely to be

### 4.1 Graphitic-N Group:

Structural property and formation: In graphene, each sp2 hybridized carbon atom bonds

with three other carbon atoms to form the hexagonal lattice. Upon nitrogen doping, when a

nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom of the graphene’s hexagonal unit it is commonly

referred to as substitutional nitrogen or graphitic-N functional group. This type of

substitutional bond brings a slight structural distortion in the lattice as the C-N bond is 0.002

nm shorter than the C-C bond [128]. N-doped sites are little protruded from the graphene

plane; It was found from the Zhao et al. measurement that the protrusion is about 0.03

Å, which is derived from the difference of the C-C and C-N bond lengths with reference

to the Cu (111) substrate. They attributed such topological features to the pure electronic

effect of doped nitrogen [127]. Intuitively it is understandable that to form graphitic-N bonds,

first, it is necessary to create carbon atom vacancies in the graphene lattice or pre-existing

vacancies should be present. Then, the nitrogen atoms produced through the decomposition

of nitrogen precursors should make bonds with the carbon atoms adjacent to vacancies and

subsequently repair the hexagonal structure. Li et al. performed ab initio molecular dynamic

simulations at experimental conditions to elucidate the formation dynamics of the graphitic-N

group on the N-G materials. Their study simulated the process of post doping of graphene by

thermal treatment at 700 – 1000 ⁰C in the presence of ammonia (NH3). They concluded that

only specific structural defects with required electronic structures on the N-G surface are

capable of trapping nitrogen atoms to form the graphitic-N group and simultaneously heal the

graphene structure. They distinguished single vacancy and particular double vacancy to have

such ability [129]. The presence of such vacancy defects in the carbon precursors produced

by conventional methods is not common. However, for the cases of post nitrogen doping by

high-energy plasma or ion beam irradiation on graphene, because of the high energy of the

particles, it is possible to generate the favorable vacancy defects by knocking off the carbon

atoms from the lattice [125].

Dependence on synthesis environment: Synthesis parameters as temperature, pressure,

precursors used, the strength of plasma, grinding speed and time, etc. play a significant role

in determining the type of nitrogen bonding configurations that could be produced. Many

research groups worked to achieve control over the formation of the nitrogen functional

groups so that they can be employed in targeted applications. Zheng et al. prepared nitrogen-

doped graphene by a hydrothermal reduction of GO with urea. Thermal annealing at 600 ⁰C

of the substance for 0.5 hours was followed. They reported that upon the thermal annealing

the graphitic-N content increased from 7.9% to a promising 36.3%. At the same time, the

percentage of the pyrrolic-N group substantially reduces. They postulated that the thermal

annealing process at 600 ⁰C can convert a significant portion of pyrrolic-N into graphitic-N

configuration [13]. While investigating the effects of pulsed ion beams of various energy

density and pulse number on the electronic structure of nitrogen atoms of n-doped

multiwalled carbon nanotubes (CNx-MWCNTs), Korusenko et al. discovered that upon the

irradiation of ion beams on CNx-MWCNTs the overall nitrogen content reduces but the

percentage of graphitic-N increases significantly. They concluded that as the ion beams

increase the surface temperature of the CNx-MWCNTs up to around 800 – 2100 ⁰C, a

portion of pyrrolic-N and pyridinic-N configurations are converted into the graphitic-N

group. They also noted that the graphitic-N configuration can remain stable up to 2200 ⁰C

[130]. As N-Gs hold similar characteristics as CNx-MWCNTs, upon ion beam irradiation

similarly changes in the bonding configurations in N-G may be possible. Yang et al. prepared

N-G samples by a one-step hydrothermal reaction of GO and urea and then this N-G was

subjected to a thermal treatment at 700 ⁰C, 800 ⁰C, and 900 ⁰C to produced different N-G

samples with various nitrogen contents. They reported that the percentage of the graphitic-N

group varied with temperature but did not follow a linear relationship [131]. Zhuang et al.

produced N-G catalysts by nanoscale high energy wet (NHEW) ball milling method for ORR

in the electrochemical systems. Grinding speed and time were identified as the controlling

perimeters for different nitrogen functional groups. They showed that with increasing

grinding time, the relative percentage of graphitic-N increases in the sample [73]. From the

studies above, it can be estimated that graphitic-N configuration forms at relatively higher

temperatures, often converted from the pyrrolic and pyridinic-N groups. However, any

generalized formation temperature rand for graphitic-N could be identified as the formation

of nitrogen bonds is critically influenced by the overall synthesis environment.

Bonding configuration and electronic effect: The contribution of graphitic-N bonds in the

local electronic structure of N-G nanomaterials is significant [129–135]. Having the atomic

number 7, the nitrogen atom possesses an extra electron than the carbon atom, where five

electrons stay in the valence cell. When a nitrogen atom substitutes one sp2 hybridized carbon

atom in the graphene lattice, it forms σ bonds with three neighboring carbon atoms with three

valence electrons. One electron joins the π system of the lattice, and the last electron enters

the conduction band and produces a strong n-type effect in the material [130,136–138]. A

schematic of the molecular orbital structure is shown in Fig. 4. Schiros et al. conducted

density functional theory (DFT) calculations for extended graphene sheet with 1%

dopants/defects of different types to access the changes in the work function and

contributions to fractional charge by each dopant configurations per N atom. Their results

show that on average 0.54 electron charge is added to the π network of the lattice by each

graphitic-N bond and the work function is reduced compared to pristine graphene [139]. The

change in the electronic structure of graphene by graphitic-N dopant is also represented

by the upward shift of the Fermi energy level near the Dirac point. When the Fermi

energy level is above the Direct point electron population in the valency band increases

which causes an excess charge distribution in the π-states of the carbon atoms of

graphene. This phenomenon manifests as an n-type doping effect in the material. Ketabi

et al. showed that for graphitic-N dopant graphene’s Fermi level shifts approximately

+0.5 eV above the Dirac point which is consistent with findings of Schiros et al. and Wu

et al. [139–141]. However, Joucken et al. pointed out that the actual electron population

of the conduction band of graphene with graphitic-N dopant is commonly

underestimated because of the use of rigid band approximation to determine the

*Fig. 4: Molecular orbital structure of the graphitic-N bond configuration.*


<!-- Page 22 -->

number of electrons in the conduction band. The rigid band approximation adopts the

assumption analogs to the conventional semiconductor where each dopant donates one

electron as the doner level below does not perturb the conduction band. Jouchen et al.

mentioned that this assumption does not hold true for graphitic-N doped graphene

because the Fermi level already shifts above the Dirac point because of the graphitic-N

dopant. They proposed that a tight-binding model can provide a more reliable result

[142].

Such change in the carrier concentration and electronic structure by the graphitic-N group

provides the material different interesting properties. For instance, Błoński et al.

demonstrated that over 5 at. % of nitrogen doping in graphene can generate ferromagnetic

property below 69 K temperature. Graphitic-N plays a pivotal role to achieve this

ferromagnetic state through significant change in the graphene’s electronic structure [132].

Catalytic activity: One of the major applications of N-G nanomaterials is its function as an

electrochemical catalyst, especially for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). The first major

step of the ORR mechanism is the chemisorption of oxygen on the catalyst surface,

specifically, on the catalytic active sites [143]. Many research groups reported that among the

nitrogen functional groups in N-Gs graphitic-N is the key for ORR catalysis. Although some

other groups proposed pyridinic-N to be the most effective catalytic center on N-Gs, opinions

based on the research findings favor graphitic-N more compellingly catalytic activity. In N-G

nanocatalysts, for graphitic-N bond configurations, the most speculated active sites are the

carbon atoms neighboring the nitrogen dopant. The reactivity of the graphitic-N based on

their locations on the N-G material’s plane appears as another point of discussion. Based on

quantum chemical calculations Sidik et al. reported that on N-G material’s, edge-adjacent

graphitic-N dopants are less reactive as they become passive in the presence of other radicles.

But, their study did not account for the ORR steps [144]. However, several groups presented

evidence supporting the highest reactivity of the graphitic-N groups located at the edges of N-

G for ORR mechanisms [145–147]. Bao et al. performed DFT calculations to investigate if

the position of the doped graphitic-N in the graphene plane has any effect on the O2

adsorption (which is the initial step for ORR) on the active sites (neighboring carbon atoms)

and subsequent ORR mechanism. Their findings showed that the graphitic-N groups located

at the zigzag edges of the N-G plane are most energetically favorable for O2 adsorption than

the other ones bonded located inside the plane [145].

### 4.2 Pyridinic-N Group:

Bonding configuration and electronic distribution: Asides from substitutional/graphitic-N,

one of the most observed nitrogen bonding configurations in N-G materials is pyridinic-N.

When doped nitrogen atom bonds with two sp2 hybridized carbon atoms of the graphene

lattice and form a pyridine-like six-membered structure, the bonding configuration is referred

to as the pyridinic-N functional group. The distribution of electrons in this bonding

configuration was studied by many groups both experimentally and theoretically. In the

pyridinic-N configuration, two of the five valance electrons of the nitrogen atom form σ

bonds with two carbon atoms, one electron joins the π-bonding system of the graphene. The

remaining two electrons stay in the nitrogen atom as lone pair electrons in the orbital oriented

along the plane of graphene. Because of this bonding configuration pyridinic-N causes

unique electron distribution locally. From the structural point of view, pyridinic-N always

accompanies carbon vacancy defects or forms at the edges of the carbon lattice. Because of

the adjacent vacancy of the nitrogen atom, there evolves a shortage of electrons in the π-

bonding system compared to the pristine graphene structure. This shortage of electrons

generates a p-type doping effect in graphene [148]. Usachov et al. experimentally observed

the same structural properties of pyridinic-N configurations [149]. Fig. 5 shows a schematic

of the molecular orbital structure of the pyridinic-N bond configuration. The investigation of

Kondo et al. of pyridinic-N configuration suggested that the lone pair of the pyridinic-N

group create an electronic state where the nitrogen atom is partially negatively charged which

renders the surrounding carbon atoms be charged positively which is also responsible for

inducing the p-type effect [128]. The effect of the pyridinic-N group on the electronic

band structure of graphene is also presented in terms of a shift in the Fermi energy level

in the vicinity of the Dirac point. Ketabi et al. showed that the Fermi level shifts

<!-- Page 24 -->

approximately -0.5 eV downward from Dirac point because of the pyridinic-N dopant

on graphene [140]. This means, unlike graphitic-N, pyridinic-N adds vacancies of

electrons in graphene’s π-network which induces the p-type effect on the material.

Lin et al. observed that pyridinic-N groups can exist in a high local N density. From close

observation of it was found that triggered by the high energy electron beam from the

spectrometer nitrogen atom of the pyridinic-N can oscillate between identical sites of the

vacancy defect. [125].

Catalytic activity: The contribution of the nitrogen atom of N-G nanocatalysts during ORR is

the point of fundamental debate among the research groups. Different interpretations of the

experimental and theoretical works on N-G nanocatalysts as ORR catalysts create obscurity.

The exact catalytic role of the nitrogen functional groups in ORR is still not agreed upon. In a

general picture, some groups showed pieces of evidence in favor of pyridinic-N as an

efficient ORR site, while other groups championed the role of graphitic-N for ORR. Xing et

al. reported when N-Gs are synthesized from multilayer graphene by ammonia hydroxide

treatment, •OH (a major ORR intermediate) preferentially adsorbed on the carbon atoms

adjacent to the nitrogen atoms in pyridinic-N configuration. According to their data, before

and after ORR, the content of graphitic-N did not change. Hence, they deduced that the

pyridine-N group plays the key catalytic role in ORR instead of the graphitic-N [150].

However, they did not provide clear evidence in favor of the 4e- pathway of ORR by the

pyridine-N. Wu et al. also identified the carbon atoms neighboring the nitrogen atom of

pyridinic-N configuration as the active site. They found that the N-G sample with the highest

pyridinic-N content shows the best ORR performance. Their results insisted that the N-G

samples with the pyridinic-N group’s dominance follow a 4e- path for ORR [9]. Miao et al.

synthesized N-G samples by a hydrothermal method and reported that upon thermal

annealing pyrrolic-N group converts into pyridinic-N. Also, they concluded the increased

pyridinic-N groups enhance the ORR catalytic activity [10]. In addition, Sun et al. reported

that the average electron transfer number and onset potential are proportional to the pyridinic-

N content [11]. Zhang et al. studied the ORR mechanism for N-G materials in an acidic

environment with DFT. The N-G models were built with pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-N

configurations. The simulation shows that the N-G models with the pyridinic-N group have

the electrocatalytic property and the ORR mechanism can proceed through the 4e- pathway.

In the pyridinic-N configuration, spin density distribution and atomic charge distribution

caused by the presence of the N atom create the catalytic active site at the neighboring carbon


<!-- Page 25 -->


25

atoms. The carbon atoms with the highest positive spin densities are the most active catalytic

sites [151].

Although many studies on the nitrogen functional groups proposed that pyridinic-N could be

the effective catalytic center for ORR in the electrochemical reactions, compelling counter

findings also have been reported. Luo et al. synthesized single layer nitrogen-doped graphene

with pure pyridinic-N and investigated its electronic structure and electrochemical properties.

The rotating disk electrode (RDE) voltammetry of oxygen reduction on their highest

performing N-G sample provided that the electron transfer number is 2. That indicated that

pyridinic-N bonding configuration may not be a promising catalyst for ORR [85]. They

attributed the low ORR performance on the lone pair electrons in the nitrogen atom of the

pyridinic-N configuration. The lone pair electrons of nitrogen join in a repulsive interaction

with the incoming O2 molecules (toward neighboring carbon) with a high density of lone pair

electrons. They also pointed out that different research groups reported ORR performances

for N-G materials with the pyridinic-N group differently and a possible reason for such

deviations is the reported binding energies of pyridinic-N, which varied in the range 398.3-

399.3 eV. In 2019, to mitigate the problem of assigning observed binding energies to a

specific function group of nitrogen, Lazar et al. proposed corrected spectroscopic fingerprints

for the major nitrogen functional groups in N-G materials. They assigned the X-ray

photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) N 1s binding energy 397.9 eV for the pyridinic-N

configuration [152].

From the studies conducted so far on the nitrogen functional groups, still it is unclear which

bonding configuration plays the vital role to catalyze ORR in the electrochemical systems.

Convincing experimental evidence and theoretical studies found to support the efficient

catalytic activity of both pyridinic-N and graphitic-N groups, although the studies followed

different methodology, test environment, and ways of interpreting the data. Nevertheless, for

now, it is clear that among all the nitrogen bonding configurations pyridinic-N and graphitic-

N groups can be the major sites for ORR catalysis. To reach a definitive conclusion over the

exact functionalities of the pyrrolic-N and graphitic-N, broad-scale studies are required.

### 4.3 Pyrrolic-N Group:

Bonding configuration and dependence on synthesis environment: Pyrrolic-N is also one of

the commonly occurring and influential nitrogen bonding configurations on the N-G

materials. When the doped nitrogen atom bonds with two carbon atoms of the graphene

lattice forming a pyrrole-like five-membered heterocyclic ring, it is commonly referred to as

the pyrrolic-N functional group. In the C-N bonds of the pyrrolic-N group, nitrogen atoms are

sp2 hybridized. In this site nitrogen atom’s two sp2 orbitals from σ bonds with two carbon

atoms with two electrons. One electron stays in the other sp2 orbital and can be protonated.

This electron could also be responsible for inducing a pseudocapacitance property in N-Gs.

Two other electrons in the unhybridized p orbital join the π conjugate system of graphene

lattice. Pyrrolic-N configuration formed near a single vacancy adjusts the deficiency of

electron in the π-system created by that vacancy with these two donated p-electrons

[138,149,153,154]. Being the five-membered ring, the pyrrolic-N group itself is a defect for

the hexagonal graphene lattice system. A schematic of the molecular orbital structure on

pyrrolic-N bond configuration is shown in Fig. 6.

Many research groups reported that pyrrolic-N group content reduces upon thermal

annealing. This suggests that pyrrolic-N bonds are not thermally stable and convert into other

bonding configurations upon thermal treatment [10]. Because of potential applicability,

different research groups synthesized N-G materials with pyrrolic-N dominance by

optimizing the synthesis parameters. Li et al. synthesized pyrrolic-N doped graphene with the

atmospheric pressure CVD method. They pointed out that a high ammonia flow rate (nitrogen

source) compared to the carbon source, high temperature of 1000 ⁰C, and growth pressure

contributed to the formation of pyrrolic-N rich N-G [155]. As mentioned earlier, Akada et al.

and Rybin et al. showed that for synthesis by plasma treatment longer plasma exposure time

## 5. Review on the Stability of N-G nanocatalyst:

One of the major goals of graphene-based electrocatalyst research is to replace the platinum-

based catalysts that are commonly used now [18,159,160]. Platinum is susceptible to CO

poisoning and time-dependent degradation. Nonetheless, the high cost of platinum is another

big issue that affects the economy of electrochemical energy generation and storage systems.

According to the cost analysis of the fuel cell system for transportation conducted through the

Department of Energy (DOE) in 2000, 67% of the Membrane Electrolyte Assembly (MEA)

solely arises from the electrode materials [161]. Because of these reasons large scale

utilization of fuel cell technology is not economical yet. With significant potential, N-G

materials became a strong candidate to replace the Pt-based catalyst from the electrochemical

systems. Numerous research groups reported that N-G catalysts can perform better in ORR in

terms of current density output than platinum-based catalysts in the same experimental

environments. However, the stability of the N-G nanocatalyst still a major concern. The

research groups reported the stability tests for their N-G samples in different manners in

terms of chosen potential range, the environment of ORR (alkaline or acidic electrolytes), the


<!-- Page 29 -->


29

number of test cycles or duration of tests, etc. The Fuel Cell Technologies Office of DOE

targeted to achieve the durability of 8,000 hours for hydrogen fuel cell power system for

transportation and 60,000 hours of durability for natural gas-operated micro-combined heat

and power (CHP) fuel cell system (5 kW) [162]. To accommodate this goal, research on N-G

nanocatalysts should provide more focus on their long-term stability in the ORR

environments. To date, studied on N-G catalyst’s durability up to that targeted range not

available, most of them conducted the stability tests in a much lower range or less harsh ORR

environments.

Stability tests in the alkaline electrolyte:

The majority of studies on stability tests of N-G nanocatalysts selected electrolyte is 0.1 M

KOH solution in N2 or O2 saturated conditions [18,134,163–169]. This ORR environment

represents the condition for alkaline fuel cells. While a nitrogen saturated environment is

used to assess the durability of catalysts in the absence of ORR species, in the oxygen

saturated environment degradation due to ORR can be identified; these approaches are

similar in fuel research [134,170,171]. Qu et al. synthesized N-G films employing a modified

Degradation mechanism of N-G nanocatalysts:

The degradation of N-G nanocatalysts is one of the key issues impeding its large-scale

application. From experimental realizations, degradation by chemical reactions is more

severe than the thermal degradation of the N-G materials. During the electrochemical

reactions, the reaction intermediates can react with the doped nitrogen atoms or the adjacent

carbon atoms. In both cases, the nitrogen atoms could be carried away from the catalytic

active sites and result in the loss of catalytic performance of N-G. Naumov et al. focused on

the degradation of N-G catalyst through the formation of ammonia (NH3) during the

electrochemical reactions [172].

N-G + n e- + n H+ → G + NH3

Here n is the number of electrons (e--) and proton (H+) transferred. They investigated three

possible paths of reaction of N-G with e- and H+ by calculating the reaction enthalpies (ΔH)

and Gibbs free energies of reaction (ΔG) for each step of all three possible paths using DFT

B3LYP method.

Path a): Electron transfer and protonation

N-G + e- → N-G-

N-G- + H+ → N-G-H

Path b): Hydrogen addition (considering e- and H+ first recombine and then adsorbed onto the

catalytic sites, which is a very fast reaction).

N-G + H• → N-G-H

Path c): e- transfer from O2- and introduction of H+:

N-G + O2•- → N-G- + O2

N-G- + H+ → N-G-H

From the calculations, it was found that with the lowest reaction enthalpy and Gibbs free

energy path b is energetically more favorable than the other paths. This also indicates that the

adsorption of hydrogen atoms on the N-G surface is even more likely than the oxidation of N-

G. However, Singh et al. mentioned if the ORR proceeds through the 2e- pathway, oxidation

of metal-free N-G catalyst is more likely [143].


<!-- Page 34 -->

Naumov et al. further investigated the effect of different nitrogen functional groups in the

degradation mechanism. Following path b, they calculated the Gibbs free energy for each of

pyridinic-N, pyrrolic-N, and graphitic-N bonding configurations in all possible pathways.

Data suggested that graphitic-N bonding configuration has the lowest possibility of

degradation through ammonia formation. And pyrrolic-n bonding configuration is most

susceptible to degradation which agrees with the literature.

## 6. Conclusion:

A review is conducted on N-G nanomaterials focusing on the overall chemical structure and

stability during the catalytic reaction. An in-detailed review is presented on the structural

properties of the common precursor materials, physical characteristics of N-G nanomaterials,

effects of N-G synthesis parameters, the chemical structure of N-G to the molecular level,

properties of major nitrogen functional groups of N-G, catalytic stability, as well as

degradation mechanism. N-Gs inherit basic structural form from their carbon precursor

materials, especially in the post-doping methods. The most accepted structure of precursor

material GO was provided by Gao et al. According to this model, in GO, the graphene plane

adsorbs different functional groups: five- and six-membered lactol (O-C-O) rings, ester of

tertiary alcohol, hydroxyl, epoxy, and ketone. The structural and electronic effects of these

adsorbed oxygen functionalities distort the GO plane. The dynamic structural model (DSM)

of GO described that the structure undergoes gradual changes in aqueous solutions. In rGO, a

considerable portion of oxygen functionalities is reduced from the surface upon thermal

treatments. However, such a reduction process can not fully restore the defectless hexagonal

honeycomb structure of pristine graphene. For N-G nanomaterials production, nitrogen

precursors are generally chosen depending on the synthesis method. To the bare eyes, N-G

materias are black/ash-colored powered material that is soluble in water. To the molecular

level, N-Gs have a crumpled film-like structure with a variety of defects on them. Along with

the structural defects, the nitrogen functional groups on the N-G plane change the electronic

structure of the material and induces different electronic properties, including the strong

ability to catalyze the ORR in the electrochemical systems. Structural details and different

favorable synthesis environments for each of the major nitrogen functional groups are

elucidated. It was found that the accurate functionalities of these nitrogen functional groups

are still largely debated. So far, we can only say that for particular synthesis processes, with a


<!-- Page 35 -->


35

specific environment and specific testing setup, one functional group can exhibit better ORR

activity over another. However, it can be deduced that the graphitic-N and pyridinic-N

bonding configurations are the key sites for ORR catalysis on N-G nanomaterials. Although

many research groups reported long-term stability studies for N-G nanocatalysts, more

rigorous attempts are necessary to reach a clear conclusion on its catalytic activity, including

tougher test conditions and more extended test periods. DFT studies could identify the

degradation mechanism of the N-G nanocatalyst’s active sites. Adsorption of hydrogen atoms

on the carbon atoms neighboring the nitrogen atoms most possibly initiate the degradation

process. The study also shows that the graphitic-N is more resistive to the degradation

process than other nitrogen bond configurations. However, compelling experimental

investigations are required to uncover a holistic view of the degradation process.
